Omitting the React `key` prop on `GrafanaRuleListItem` in the filtered list breaks reconciliation and can produce stale UI when results change. Add `key={key}` to the `GrafanaRuleListItem` element.

`canPause` and `canDelete` include promRule abilities, but the Pause item is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` and the Delete item on `rulerRule` being truthy, so list-view users with promRule permissions see no items. Either restrict pause/delete ability checks to rulerRule availability or implement promRule-based handlers and drop the rulerRule-only render guards.

The silence drawer only mounts when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, yet in the list view `rule` is undefined and the Silence menu item is shown from promRule abilities, so clicking it does nothing. Render the drawer from `promRule` when available, or hide the Silence item when no drawer can be opened.

`useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` calls `useFolder` via both `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` and `useCanSilenceInFolder` for every Grafana rule in the list, creating two RTK Query subscriptions per rule. Move folder permission/silence lookups to the group level or memoize by folder UID to keep subscription count proportional to folders, not rules.

issues.descricao: The pause menu item is still gated on a Grafana ruler rule, but the list view now passes only the Prometheus rule, so Pause/Resume disappears for list-view rules even when the user may pause them.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based pause ability cannot display Pause or Resume for list-view rules because the menu still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) before rendering MenuItemPauseRule. GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies only promRule, so these actions disappear even for editable rules. Adapt the pause menu item to accept the Grafana identifier and Prometheus pause state, or load the ruler rule on demand.

issues.descricao: The Delete menu item still requires a ruler rule, which list-view Grafana rules no longer provide, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based delete ability is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule` when rendering the Delete item. Both Grafana list-view paths now omit rulerRule, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action entirely. Render deletion using the available identifier and group identifier instead of requiring the ruler DTO, adapting the callback contract accordingly.

issues.descricao: When the Grafana prom-rule branch is skipped (datasource rules), useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) still reports Duplicate as supported and allowed by Grafana create permission, and AlertRuleMenu ORs it with the ruler ability, so Duplicate appears on cloud rules even when the ruler check denies it.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: canDuplicate ORs ruler ability with grafana ability where grafana path is skipToken=>undefined for cloud rules, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) returns Duplicate=[true,true] whenever the user has global Grafana create permission. WHY: Any user with Grafana rule-create gets Duplicate menu item on cloud/Mimir rules even when ruler abilities deny it — incorrect authorization gating. HOW: Return NotSupported for all abilities when rule is skipToken/undefined, or gate grafana branch on prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) before ORing.

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities returns AlwaysSupported for Duplicate when rule is undefined (skipToken): loading is false from the !rule early-return, so MaybeSupported=true and duplicateSupported=true. ORed in AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons this leaks Grafana create permission into non-Grafana rules. Gate MaybeSupported/duplicateSupported on rule existence (e.g. NotSupported when !rule).

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities must return NotSupported for all actions when rule is undefined (skipToken). Currently MaybeSupported falls back to AlwaysSupported when !loading, so Duplicate=[true, global-create] is true for a cloud rule passed as skipToken, and AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons OR-logic then incorrectly enables Duplicate (and Explore). Guard with if (!rule) return all-NotSupported abilities or make MaybeSupported require rule.

issues.descricao: The refactor of useAllAlertRuleAbilities into useAllRulerRuleAbilities drops the isFederatedRuleGroup check (isFederated is hardcoded false), so federated Mimir rules are reported as editable and deletable.

comentarios.texto: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated = false. The previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check is gone, so federated Mimir rules are no longer treated as immutable and can show edit and delete abilities. Keep the federation check in this wrapper, or pass the federation state into the shared hook.

Delegating useAllAlertRuleAbilities to useAllRulerRuleAbilities discards the group's federation status and replaces the previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check with a constant false. Legacy RuleActionsButtons consequently enables editing rules in groups with source_tenants, although these groups were explicitly immutable before this change. Preserve the CombinedRule federation check in the wrapper or pass federation status into the delegated ability calculation.

Preserve the federated-group immutability check when delegating this CombinedRule hook. Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities inspected rule.group with isFederatedRuleGroup and disabled modification/removal for federated rules. The replacement delegates to a hook that hardcodes isFederated=false and receives no group information. Existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities consumers therefore now receive supported update/delete abilities for federated rules when datasource permissions allow them, exposing operations that the previous contract explicitly prohibited. Pass the federation state through or retain that restriction in this wrapper.

issues.descricao: The Grafana prom-rule abilities gate Pause, Restore, Export and DeletePermanently on alertingRule(rule) while the comment claims it checks Grafana-managed rules, so Grafana recording rules lose these actions in the list view.

comentarios.texto: The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the variable it describes is `isAlertingRule`. That variable is true only for alerting rules and false for Grafana recording rules. Fix the comment, or rename the variable, so it says the check is for alerting rules. As written, readers will expect Pause, Export and Silence to be enabled for recording rules.

The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the check used is alertingRule(rule), which is false for recording rules. Pause, Restore, ModifyExport and DeletePermanently are therefore wrongly disabled for Grafana recording rules, where the old isGrafanaManagedAlertRule check allowed them. comentarios.texto: The comment says there is no loading state, but the next line is `loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported`. `loading` comes from the folder fetch. Update the comment to say that support depends on the folder loading state.

issues.descricao: The Grafana branch of the filtered rule list renders GrafanaRuleListItem without a key prop, so React reconciles the streaming list by index and warns about missing keys.
issues.textoGolden: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

WHAT: Grafana branch of FilterViewResults renders GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key} while datasource and unknown branches pass key. issues.descricao: The test named 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks the More button exists, never the menu options.

It finds the button by name 'More', so the aria-label and text assertions are tautological. It would pass even if the menu had no actions or the abilities were broken. Click the button and assert the expected menu items, or rename the test to match what it checks.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never opens the menu nor asserts menu items — it only checks More button presence/aria/text. Click More and assert expected menuitems (or rename to 'should render More button') so it fails if menu actions break.

The documentation describes a data source the function no longer consumes; update it to state only the Prometheus endpoint is loaded (and the same stale "Ruler response" reference in the expectedRulesCount prop doc at lines 18–19 should be corrected).

issues.descricao: For list-view Grafana rules RuleActionsButtons gets only promRule, so the Silence menu item is shown but the silence drawer, still gated on a ruler alerting rule, never renders and clicking Silence does nothing.
issues.textoGolden: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

comentarios.texto: Passing only promRule enables the Silence notifications menu item but leaves RuleActionsButtons.V2 unable to render its silence drawer, which is guarded by rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). Clicking Silence only updates showSilenceDrawer and displays nothing because rule is undefined. Update the drawer to accept a rule UID—the inspected SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only needs grafana_alert.uid—and allow the Prometheus alerting-rule path to render it.

The new list item passes only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, but that component renders SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only under `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. With rule undefined, clicking the newly enabled 'Silence notifications' action only sets state and never opens a drawer. Adapt the silence rendering path to load/use the rule by its Prometheus identifier before switching this caller to promRule-only.

WHAT: getEditableIdentifier now enables a prom-only path (Grafana uid identifier with rulerRule undefined) but the silence drawer still renders only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. WHY: In the list view Silence menu item can be shown via grafana abilities, clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer but the drawer never mounts, so Silence silently does nothing. sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The GitHub OAuth `state` parameter is set to `pipeline.signature`, a deterministic md5 hash of pipeline view class names. WHY: An attacker can predict the state value and craft a callback URL that the victim's pipeline will accept, bypassing OAuth2 CSRF protection. HOW: Generate a per-session nonce with `secrets.token_hex()`, bind it to pipeline state with `pipeline.bind_state("state", state)`, pass it in the authorize redirect, and compare `request.GET.get("state")` against `pipeline.fetch_state("state")` on callback, matching the existing OAuth2LoginView/OAuth2CallbackView pattern in sentry/identity/oauth2.py.

WHAT: `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without checking that the `"sender"` key exists. WHY: Integrations created before this change or through code paths that omit `metadata["sender"]` will raise `KeyError` and crash the installation pipeline instead of returning the intended error page. HOW: Guard the access the same way `installation.py` does: fail closed with `return error(request, self.active_organization)` when `"sender"` is missing or when `login` is absent.

WHAT: `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` uses `pipeline.signature` as the GitHub OAuth `state` parameter and verifies the returned `state` against the same constant. WHY: `pipeline.signature` is an MD5 hash of the pipeline view class names and is identical for every request, so an attacker can know or forge the `state` and force a victim’s Sentry session to accept an attacker-controlled GitHub authorization code, bypassing OAuth CSRF protection. HOW: Generate `state` with `secrets.token_hex()`, store it with `pipeline.bind_state("state", state)`, and compare the callback against `pipeline.fetch_state("state")`, matching `OAuth2CallbackView`.

WHAT: `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without checking that the `sender` key exists. WHY: `build_integration` only stores `metadata["sender"]` when the incoming state already has a sender (integration.py:376), so pre-existing integrations or installations created without that webhook field lack the key and raise `KeyError` instead of failing gracefully. HOW: Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a mismatch that returns the existing `error` response.

WHAT: The POST to GitHub’s access-token endpoint only sends `code`, `client_id`, and `client_secret`, omitting `redirect_uri` even though it was included in the authorization request. WHY: GitHub requires the same `redirect_uri` in the token exchange when one was supplied during authorization, so the exchange can be rejected and the installation pipeline will fail. HOW: Add `"redirect_uri": redirect_uri` to the `data` dictionary, reusing the same `redirect_uri` used for the authorize URL.

issues.descricao: error() calls _(error_short) on a variable and callers pass plain literals, so the short error strings are no longer extractable for translation.

comentarios.texto: The helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. The translation extractor cannot see these strings, so the short error messages sent to the user are no longer translatable; the old code wrapped the literals directly in `_()`. Mark the literals with gettext_lazy at the call sites and the default, and pass them through without wrapping again.

error_short strings bypass translation extraction: _(error_short) uses a variable so makemessages cannot collect them. Wrap literals at definition/call sites, e.g. error_short=_("Invalid installation request.") and pass _("...") literals, then use data error value directly without re-wrapping.

Translate the short-message literals at their definition/call sites instead of calling `_(error_short)` on a variable. Django's message extraction cannot extract the default `"Invalid installation request."` or the plain-string arguments at the two call sites from this dynamic gettext invocation. The existing pending-deletion and already-installed messages previously appeared directly inside `_()`; this refactor removes their extraction sites, and the new default message cannot enter translation catalogs. Use a translated default and translated arguments, then place `error_short` directly into the payload so these user-facing errors remain localizable.

issues.descricao: The org parameter of error()/get_document_origin is actually the active-organization context, not an Organization, so the name is misleading.

comentarios.texto: The parameter is named `org` but the code treats it as the pipeline's active-organization context: it dereferences `org.organization` and every caller (error() and the GitHubInstallation sites) passes `self.active_organization`, not an Organization. The name misstates the argument's type/contract — a caller following the name and passing a real Organization would hit AttributeError on `.organization`. Rename the parameter (e.g. `active_organization`) and correct the corresponding name in `error()` at line 131 so the two signatures match what is actually passed.

issues.descricao: The GitHub OAuth state is pipeline.signature, a static md5 of the pipeline view names, instead of a per-attempt random nonce, so it gives no CSRF protection.
issues.textoGolden: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

comentarios.texto: The OAuth state is pipeline.signature, which Pipeline.__init__ computes solely from pipeline view class names and therefore shares across all users and installation attempts. An attacker can obtain an OAuth code for their own GitHub account and send a callback using this known state to a victim with an active installation pipeline, binding the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's flow instead of rejecting the forged callback. Generate a random per-attempt nonce, store it in pipeline state, and validate that nonce on the OAuth callback.

Do not use pipeline.signature as OAuth state. It is a deterministic MD5 of the pipeline identifiers, not an unpredictable nonce tied to this user's authorization attempt (the tests reuse it across users). An attacker can know the expected state and submit a callback containing a code authorized under the attacker's GitHub account, defeating the OAuth login-CSRF protection and the intended binding to the installing user. Generate a cryptographically random per-attempt state, store it in the session/pipeline, and validate and consume it on callback.

issues.descricao: The new OAuth step's token exchange and user lookup are not wrapped in error handling, so GitHub/network failures surface as 500s instead of the installation-failed page.

comentarios.texto: The token request is executed outside the try block. If GitHub's token endpoint is unavailable or the request fails with a connection/timeout error, safe_urlopen raises before the guarded response parsing is reached, and this new installation step returns an unhandled server error instead of the installation-failed response. Include the request itself in the error handling and handle the relevant transport exceptions.

WHAT: safe_urlopen token exchange and get_user_info() (which calls resp.raise_for_status()) are called with no exception handling. WHY: Any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from GitHub bubbles up as an unhandled exception and 500s the install instead of rendering the invalid-request page. HOW: Wrap the exchange plus get_user_info in try/except and return error() on failure.

safe_urlopen() and get_user_info() are called outside any try/except, so network errors, non-2xx responses, or API failures raise unhandled exceptions instead of returning error(). Wrap the token exchange + user-info fetch in try/except and return error() on failure, matching the handled missing-access_token path.

issues.descricao: When no Integration exists yet for the installation_id the pipeline advances without comparing the OAuth user to the installer, bypassing the new ownership check.

comentarios.texto: The missing Integration branch advances the pipeline without verifying that github_authenticated_user installed the supplied installation_id. When the installation webhook has not created a record, or the local record was deleted, finish_pipeline calls build_integration using app credentials and attaches the installation without checking the OAuth user's access, allowing a user with another account's installation ID to bypass the new ownership check. Fail closed until trusted installer information is available and apply the ownership check before every successful next_step.

The record-absent path advances the pipeline before checking whether the authenticated GitHub user installed this app. Installation IDs arrive from the request, and a missing Integration record (for example before the installation webhook is processed) does not establish ownership. As a result, this path can attach an installation belonging to a different GitHub user despite the new authenticity check. Verify the authenticated user's authorization for the installation before advancing in this branch too, rather than relying on the webhook-created record existing.

When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the code calls next_step() without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the installer. An attacker can supply an installation_id they do not own before the installation webhook has created the row, and bypass the new verification. Do not skip the check in this branch. Either fail closed, or verify ownership another way, for example by confirming the user can access the installation through the GitHub API.

issues.descricao: The installer check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking that sender exists, raising KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.
issues.textoGolden: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

comentarios.texto: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is indexed without checking that "sender" exists, so an ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender raises KeyError (500) here. metadata["sender"] is only populated when state.get("sender") is set (integration.py:376-377), and the only writer of that state is the installation webhook (webhook.py:202-208); integrations created through the pipeline itself carry no sender (confirmed by installation.py:44 which explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`, and by the pipeline-created integration in test_integration.py:730-743). Previously this branch only bound state and called pipeline.next_step(), so this crash is newly introduced. Fix: guard the lookup, e.g. `if pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != (integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login"):` and decide the desired fallback when sender is absent.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError. build_integration (line 376-377) only sets metadata["sender"] when state.get("sender") is truthy, so an existing Integration without a sender entry makes this subscripting throw an unhandled KeyError (500) instead of routing to the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and treat a missing sender as a failed verification) so the mismatch/absence case returns error() rather than crashing.

The new ownership check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] even though GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration omits sender for normal pipeline-created integrations. Reconnecting an existing active integration without an OrganizationIntegration and without webhook-populated sender now raises KeyError and returns a server error rather than an installation failure. Handle missing sender explicitly and return the invalid-installation response when trusted installer metadata is unavailable.

issues.descricao: test_installation_not_found uses a wrong OAuth state, so it fails at the state check and never reaches the installation-not-found path it is meant to test.

comentarios.texto: First response (installation_id) is overwritten by second response (bad state) with no assertion, so the Integration.DoesNotExist / not-ACTIVE branch in GitHubInstallation is never verified. Keep/assert the first flow through a valid OAuth step to reach the installation check instead of only asserting the OAuth state-mismatch error.

This test no longer verifies the "installation not found" path it exists for. The second GET supplies state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the github pipeline signature (that is the 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 asserted in test_github_setup and reused elsewhere). OAuthLoginView.dispatch (integration.py:412-413) therefore returns error() before GitHubInstallation runs, producing the same generic "Invalid installation request." message and the same failed template via the state-mismatch branch. The Integration.DoesNotExist handling at integration.py:493-498 is never reached, so the test would still pass if that handling were removed or broken. Use the real pipeline state so the request advances into GitHubInstallation, or assert on something that distinguishes the state-mismatch branch from the missing-installation branch.

The replacement assertion no longer verifies that a nonexistent installation is rejected: 'Invalid installation request.' is also returned for a state mismatch, missing access token, or missing authenticated login before GitHubInstallation is reached. This test can therefore pass with installation-not-found handling broken if the callback fails OAuth validation instead. Establish a successful OAuth exchange with the actual pipeline state and verify that the nonexistent installation lookup is reached and rejected, rather than accepting this shared authentication-error message alone.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code credential from the raw stored code list, so allCodesUsed() always returns false and getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() always returns the first code. WHY: This makes the UI always prompt for code 1 and prevents the framework from detecting when all recovery codes have been consumed, breaking recovery-code depletion semantics for user-storage credentials. HOW: Store the serialized credentialData and secretData produced by RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel in updateCredential, then return that stored model from getCredentials instead of re-creating it with createFromValues.

WHAT: Recovery codes are persisted as plain-text JSON in credentialData and validated by comparing the raw user input directly to the raw stored codes. WHY: Recovery codes are sensitive single-use credentials; storing and comparing them in plain text exposes them to any party with access to the user-storage backend and violates Keycloak's hashing requirement for this credential type. HOW: In updateCredential, create a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel (which hashes the codes) and persist both its credentialData and secretData; in isValid, hash the input with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode before comparing against the stored hashed codes.

WHAT: isValid only checks whether the submitted recovery code exists in the stored list and never updates the credential to mark that code as used. WHY: Recovery codes are intended to be single-use; without consuming the used code, the same code can authenticate repeatedly, bypassing the one-time semantics of recovery codes. HOW: After a successful match, remove the consumed code from the stored RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel and persist the updated credentialData/secretData back to user storage.

WHAT: After RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns a federated credential and allCodesUsed() is true, the code calls removeStoredCredentialById, which only removes credentials from local Keycloak storage. WHY: For user-storage credentials this removal silently does nothing, so the depleted credential remains and the required action to configure new codes may not behave correctly. HOW: Distinguish federated from local credentials; for federated credentials, invoke the user storage's disableCredentialType or a storage-specific deletion path instead of removeStoredCredentialById.

WHAT: The recovery-code validation path returns true when the submitted code exists in the stored list but never updates the credential to mark that code as used. WHY: Recovery codes are single-use by design; without consuming the code, the same code can be reused indefinitely and the credential is never flagged as exhausted. HOW: After a successful match, remove the matched code from the persisted list (or maintain a used-codes set) and persist the updated credential; return false if the code was already used.

WHAT: Recovery codes are persisted as a JSON array of raw strings in credentialData and validated by direct string equality. WHY: This stores single-factor backup secrets in plaintext, exposing them if the user-storage backend is compromised and bypassing the hashing that the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider uses. HOW: Hash codes with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode before storage and validate with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.verifyRecoveryCodeInput, matching the local provider's implementation.

WHAT: getCredentials rebuilds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel from the raw stored code list on every call, so all codes are always represented as unused. WHY: The login bean always reports the first code as the next one to enter, and allCodesUsed() never reflects actual consumption, breaking the single-use UX and the exhausted-credential cleanup path. HOW: Persist and restore the remaining/used state alongside the code list and use it when reconstructing the model, or remove used codes from the persisted list so the reconstructed model matches reality.

WHAT: After RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns a federated credential and allCodesUsed() is true, the authenticator calls removeStoredCredentialById, which only removes credentials from Keycloak's local/federated DB store. WHY: For credentials that actually live in an external user storage, this call does not delete the credential, so the exhausted recovery-code credential remains and the user is not forced to reconfigure. HOW: Use disableCredentialType(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE) for federated credentials, or have the user storage provider delete the credential itself when the last code is consumed.

issues.descricao: The test user-storage provider validates recovery codes without consuming the used code, so the same code can be replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

The new recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list without consuming the accepted code. Repeating a successful login with the same code succeeds indefinitely, while getCredentials reconstructs all original codes so the login form never advances or detects exhaustion. Validate the next unused code and persist its consumption before returning success.

The new federated recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list but never removes a successfully used code from myUser.recoveryCodes. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid on subsequent logins, and getCredentials reconstructs the full original set every time. Consume and persist the successfully validated code (and test a second login/replay), so federated recovery codes retain their one-time semantics.

issues.descricao: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-codes credential without copying the stored credential id, so the returned federated credential has a null id and cannot be targeted by id-based removal.
issues.textoGolden: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code model without copying the ID assigned during updateCredential. createFromValues does not assign an ID, so the exposed federated credential has a null ID and CredentialDeleteHelper cannot resolve it by the stored credential ID for account deletion. Copy myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() to the reconstructed model before returning it.

The CredentialModel returned from getCredentials for recovery codes is built with createFromValues and never gets the stored credential's id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()). RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator later calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId()) once all codes are used, and this would pass a null id. Fix: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after creating the model.

issues.descricao: Creating recovery codes in external storage does not remove a previously stored local recovery-codes credential, and validation falls back to local storage, so the replaced codes still authenticate.

comentarios.texto: Successful recovery-code creation in external storage leaves any existing locally stored recovery-code credential active. For a federated user who previously stored codes locally and now has an external provider supporting this type, regeneration no longer calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential's replacement cleanup; UserCredentialManager.isValid falls back to the local validator when external validation rejects an old code, so the supposedly replaced codes still authenticate. Remove the previous local recovery-code credential after successful external creation.

issues.descricao: Exhausted recovery codes are removed with removeStoredCredentialById, which only covers local storage, so a federated recovery-codes credential is never removed.

comentarios.texto: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but this code still calls removeStoredCredentialById() on it once all codes are used. That removal only targets local stored credentials, so a federated credential may not be removed. The user could then be left with an exhausted credential in user storage. Remove federated credentials through the federated path, or confirm the removal reaches user storage.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a credential from user storage, but exhausted codes are cleaned up with removeStoredCredentialById, which only targets the local DB. For a federated credential (possibly with a null id), the exhausted credential is never removed or the call misbehaves, so the user keeps a dead credential. Remove federated credentials through a path that covers user storage, for example by checking where the credential came from.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a federated credential. The authenticator still removes an exhausted one with removeStoredCredentialById(getId()), which only deletes from the local store, and the federated model's id may be null. Remove the credential through the path that matches where it was found, for example by checking whether it came from the federated stream and using the federated removal.

issues.descricao: Looking up recovery codes now always queries the federated provider first, which for LDAP users adds an LDAP round-trip and can throw IllegalStateException, failing recovery-code login with a 500.
An error log in the test user storage hard-codes the credential type as 'recovery-codes' instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE ('recovery-authn-codes').

The test federation provider BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage regenerates the recovery-codes model from the raw list on every getCredentials and never records consumed codes, so the next-code number and allCodesUsed() never reflect usage for its users.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: checkIfIsAvailable returns true as soon as a slot falls inside a date override, before checking the host's busy times. WHY: A fixed or round-robin host with a calendar conflict during an override availability window will still be offered for booking. HOW: Remove the early return and fall through to the busy.every check; only skip the working-hours guard when the slot is covered by an override.

WHAT: The working-hours end guard is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime. WHY: A slot that starts within working hours but extends past the day's end (e.g., 16:30 slot with 60-min length when hours end at 17:00) is incorrectly allowed for fixed hosts. HOW: Change the end calculation to use slotEndTime.hour() and slotEndTime.minute().

WHAT: The zero-length override check compares two Dayjs objects with ===. WHY: Each dayjs(...) call returns a new object, so the comparison is always false and a same-moment override (e.g., an all-day block) never marks slots unavailable. HOW: Use .isSame() to compare the two moments.

WHAT: The date-override availability check uses .find to return true when any single override places the slot outside. WHY: If a host has two overrides on the same day (e.g., 10-12 and 14-16), an 11:00 slot is inside the first override but outside the second, so it is wrongly rejected. HOW: Compute whether the slot overlaps any override and use that overlap to decide availability.

WHAT: The override timezone conversion uses override.start.toString() to feed dayjs.tz, so the parsed wall-clock time depends on the Node.js process timezone. WHY: On a server not running UTC, the same override produces different availability boundaries and can shift or drop slots. HOW: Parse the stored UTC Date's wall-clock explicitly with dayjs.utc(override.start).format(...) before interpreting it in the organizer timezone.

WHAT: checkIfIsAvailable converts override times with dayjs(date.start), which applies the Node.js runtime timezone. WHY: On a non-UTC server the computed override day and boundary can be wrong, causing slots to be accepted or rejected on the wrong day. HOW: Use dayjs.utc(date.start) and dayjs.utc(date.end) consistently so the stored UTC wall-clock is interpreted independently of runtime timezone.

WHAT: The activeOverrides filter keeps only overrides whose UTC start timestamp falls within the invitee's day. WHY: When the organizer is in a timezone ahead of the invitee, an override for the organizer's local day can start on the previous UTC day but still overlap the invitee's day, so the override is discarded and slots are missing. HOW: Replace the start-point check with an interval-overlap check against the invitee day.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check computes end from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, so slots that start within working hours but end after them are accepted.
issues.textoGolden: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` — an exact duplicate of `start` — instead of using `slotEndTime`. WHY: the working-hours upper-bound test `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore compares the slot START against the working-day end, so a slot whose start is inside working hours but whose end (start + eventLength) overruns `workingHour.endTime` is never filtered and is reported as available, allowing bookings outside the host's working hours. HOW: compute `const end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute();`.

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`, so it always equals `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` check is identical to the `start` check and never catches a slot that starts within working hours but ends past them. Use `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` for `end`.

`end` is computed identically to `start` (both from slotStartTime), so the check `start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime` can never reject a slot on the upper bound. A slot starting inside working hours but ending after workingHour.endTime is wrongly considered available; derive `end` from slotEndTime instead.

issues.descricao: The date-override check compares two dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, so zero-length (day off) overrides are never detected.
issues.textoGolden: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

comentarios.texto: This compares two separately constructed dayjs objects with `===` (reference equality), which is always false, so a zero-length override (start equal to end, whole day blocked) never returns true here. Compare timestamps, e.g. `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes'))`.

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separate dayjs object references, so `===` is always false. The zero-length date-override branch is dead code and such an override is never recognised as covering the day; compare values (e.g. .isSame() or .valueOf() === .valueOf()) instead.

The equality check compares two separately created Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false, even when the override start and end represent the same instant. The intended zero-length/closed-day rejection is unreachable, and a slot beginning exactly at that instant can reach the dateOverrideExist success return. Compare timestamps or use isSame instead.

issues.descricao: When a date override exists for the day, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before checking busy times, so slots overlapping existing bookings are reported available.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: when `dateOverrideExist` is true the function returns `true` before running the `busy.every(...)` check at the end. WHY: on any day that has a matching date override, a slot inside the override is reported available without checking the host's existing bookings (`busy` is spread via `...schedule`/`...userSchedule`), so a fixed/loose host who already has a booking during the override window is still shown as free — enabling double-booking. HOW: do not return early here; fall through so the override branch only decides whether the slot is inside the override window, and let the existing `busy` evaluation decide availability (e.g. `if (dateOverrideExist) { /* within override, still check busy */ } else { /* fall through to busy */ }`).

The new `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` short-circuits the `busy` conflict check (and the workingHours check) for any slot that falls inside a date override window. Every caller of `checkIfIsAvailable` previously counted on it returning false for a slot that overlaps an existing booking; on days covered by a date override that guarantee is gone, so slots conflicting with the user's real bookings are now reported as available and can be double-booked. The override branch should let control fall through to the `busy.every(...)` check (returning true only for the availability-window part) instead of returning early.

A matching date override returns true before checking busy periods. Both fixed-host and loose-host callers pass calendar and booking conflicts in busy, so a host with an override is offered even when an existing booking overlaps the slot. Continue to the busy checks after validating the override instead of returning true.

issues.descricao: The working-hours check rejects a slot when any interval for the weekday excludes it, so split schedules (e.g. morning and afternoon) reject all slots.

comentarios.texto: The working-hours predicate rejects a slot if any interval on its weekday does not contain it. A split schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00 therefore loses every slot, since each valid slot lies outside the other interval. Require at least one matching interval to contain the full event instead of finding an interval that excludes it.

This search rejects a slot if it falls outside any working-hours window on that weekday. With split hours of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a valid 10:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the afternoon window. Check for containment in at least one applicable window rather than finding any window that excludes the slot.

WHAT: Outside-working-hours test uses workingHours.find() returning true if ANY entry rejects the slot. WHY: With split schedules (two entries same weekday, e.g. morning+afternoon) a valid morning slot is outside the afternoon entry, find() matches and the slot is wrongly rejected as outside hours. HOW: Invert logic to accept if ANY entry contains the slot (e.g. !workingHours.some(entry contains slot) => outside).

issues.descricao: The date-override bound compares the slot start, not the slot end, with the override end, so slots extending past the override are accepted.

comentarios.texto: The override bounds reject only non-overlapping slots rather than requiring the entire event to fit inside an override. A fixed host with a 10:00–11:00 override accepts a 10:30–11:30 event generated from another host's availability, despite being unavailable for its final half hour. Accept only when at least one override contains both slotStartTime and slotEndTime; this also avoids rejecting a slot merely because another interval on the same date does not overlap it.

The upper bound checks whether slotStartTime is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override end but finishes after it is treated as available. Compare slotEndTime with the override end using isAfter, so the slot must fit entirely inside the override.

issues.descricao: The override timezone conversion keeps only hour and minute, so overrides that cross midnight in the invitee timezone become inverted ranges or are applied to the wrong day.

comentarios.texto: Timezone conversion takes only hour and minute, discarding day rollover and turning intervals crossing attendee midnight into reversed ranges. A UTC organizer's 22:00–23:00 override viewed in UTC+01:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30, which buildSlots skips because start is greater than end, removing valid availability. Preserve the converted dates and split the interval across attendee-day boundaries before building slots.

WHAT: activeOverrides are filtered by UTC day (line 206-207) before the invitee/organizer offset is applied (lines 212-224), and shifted hours are not re-bucketed across midnight. WHY: An override that shifts to the previous/next calendar day in the invitee timezone is dropped from the wrong day or applied to the wrong day, so slots show open when the organizer is off (and vice versa). HOW: Filter/bucket overrides in the invitee-local date after applying the offset, or emit split entries spanning two invitee days.

issues.descricao: The new working-hours check does not reject slots on weekdays that have no working-hours entry, so those slots are treated as available.

comentarios.texto: A weekday with no matching working-hours entry falls through to the busy checks and is treated as available when there are no conflicts. In round-robin events, slots generated for a loose host can consequently include a fixed host whose schedule excludes that day. Reject slots unless a working-hours interval on the slot's weekday contains the event, when no date override applies.

issues.descricao: checkIfIsAvailable's date-override check never rejects a slot that starts before the override start (only one that ends before it), so slots partly outside the override hours are treated as available.

The override day is computed with local-time dayjs(date.start) while the slot day is formatted in UTC, so on a server not running in UTC overrides near midnight are applied to the wrong day or skipped.
With several date-override ranges on the same day, a slot is rejected as soon as it falls outside any one of them, so slots inside the other ranges become unavailable.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The add_members action splits the comma-separated usernames parameter without trimming whitespace from each value. WHY: A value such as 'alice, bob' causes User.find_by_username(' bob') to return nil, so the user is silently omitted from the group with no feedback. HOW: Strip each username before the lookup, e.g., username.strip inside the loop.

WHAT: remove_member deletes the group membership with group.users.delete(user_id), bypassing the model's usernames= path that clears users.primary_group_id. WHY: A user removed from their primary group retains a stale primary_group_id referencing the group they no longer belong to. HOW: Clear the primary_group_id in the same operation, e.g., User.where(id: user_id, primary_group_id: group.id).update_all(primary_group_id: nil) after the deletion.

WHAT: group.users.delete(user_id) persists the membership removal immediately, but the action then calls group.save and reports render_json_error if that save fails. WHY: If an unrelated validation causes group.save to fail, the controller returns an error response even though the member has already been removed from the database. HOW: Wrap the deletion and save in a transaction so they succeed or fail atomically, or validate the group before applying the deletion.

WHAT: The next action clamps the new offset to user_count, which can lie past the last page of members. WHY: For 100 members with limit 50, clicking next from offset 50 sets offset to 100 and findMembers returns an empty list, leaving the user on an empty page 3. HOW: Clamp to the last page's starting offset with Math.min(offset + limit, Math.max(0, user_count - limit)).

WHAT: The remove_member authorization test calls xhr :put, :remove_member, but config/routes.rb maps remove_member only to DELETE. WHY: The test exercises the wrong route and will raise a routing error instead of reaching the controller, so the assertion that automatic groups return 422 is never validated. HOW: Change xhr :put to xhr :delete in the test.

WHAT: members accepts arbitrary limit and offset values without clamping. WHY: A huge limit (or limit=-1, which PostgreSQL treats as no limit) can force the server to load and serialize an unbounded number of members, and a negative offset triggers a SQL error; this also removes the previous 200-member cap for automatic groups. HOW: Clamp limit to a reasonable maximum and ensure offset is non-negative before querying.

WHAT: totalPages is computed with Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which returns one page too many when user_count is an exact multiple of limit. WHY: next clamps the new offset to user_count, so a group with 100 members and a limit of 50 navigates to offset 100 and renders an empty third page. HOW: Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit) and advance the offset by limit without clamping it to user_count.

WHAT: The addMembers action sends the selected usernames to the server but never clears the usernames property. WHY: Because the input stays populated and the button remains enabled, clicking Add again (or re-selecting the same users) re-submits the same list; the server may then try to add already-existing members and fail on the unique group_users index. HOW: Clear usernames after the server confirms the add, and guard against concurrent submissions.

issues.descricao: The admin group pager computes total pages as floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so when the member count is an exact multiple of the limit it shows an extra page and Next navigates to an empty member list.
issues.textoGolden: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

comentarios.texto: totalPages (and currentPage) use `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which is an off-by-one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 members, limit 50 → reports 2 pages although only 1 exists). This leaves `showingLast` false on the real last page, so 'next' navigates to an empty page at offset=user_count. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (and compute currentPage consistently) to get the correct page count.

totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives 2 for user_count=50, limit=50, although 50 members occupy exactly one page. Correct it to `Math.ceil(this.get('user_count') / this.get('limit'))`. Effect: for a group whose member count is a multiple of the page size, totalPages is one too high, showingLast remains false so the 'next' link stays enabled, and clicking it navigates to a phantom empty page.

`totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which over-counts by one whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with limit 50 yields 2 pages instead of 1). Since `showingLast` is `propertyEqual("currentPage", "totalPages")`, on a full last page `showingLast` is false, so the `next` action stays enabled and advances `offset` to `user_count`, rendering an empty page labeled as the last page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the zero-member guard) so the count matches the real number of pages.

issues.descricao: Several Group model functions (findMembers, destroy, userCountDisplay) return a value on some paths and undefined on others, triggering consistent-return lint warnings.
issues.textoGolden: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

issues.descricao: Paging actions fire overlapping member requests and each response unconditionally overwrites offset and members, so a stale response arriving last can revert the list to an earlier page.

comentarios.texto: Guard against stale member-fetch responses before updating the model. `next` updates offset immediately and leaves navigation enabled, so with at least three pages two rapid clicks issue requests for offsets 50 and 100. If the offset-100 response arrives first and the offset-50 response arrives last, this unconditional `setProperties` resets both offset and members to the older page, undoing the latest navigation. Refreshes after membership changes can similarly be overwritten by an earlier fetch. Track a per-model request generation and apply only the latest response, or serialize navigation and refresh requests.

issues.descricao: The public members endpoint now always caps results at 50 per page, but the public group members page has no pagination, so groups with more than 50 members are silently truncated for users.

comentarios.texto: The public members route now loads only the model's default 50-member page without providing any way to request subsequent pages. The public group/members.hbs template only renders members and has no Next/Previous controls, so members after the first 50 become inaccessible (manual groups previously returned all members). Add public pagination controls and actions that update offset and reload members.

The new default limit applies to nonautomatic groups as well, but the public group-members route still calls findMembers() only once and its template simply iterates members without pagination. Previously this endpoint returned every member of a nonautomatic group; now a group with more than 50 members exposes only the first 50 on its public members page, with no way to reach the rest. Update that consumer to fetch subsequent pages or provide pagination when introducing this endpoint contract.

Provide pagination or load subsequent pages for the public group-members view. findMembers now requests only 50 members, and this route calls it only once while its template simply iterates members without navigation. Custom groups previously returned all members, so groups larger than 50 now have members that cannot be viewed on this page.

issues.descricao: Creating a group ignores the alias_level the admin selected, saving only name and visibility, so new groups keep the default alias level.

comentarios.texto: Persist params[:alias_level] when creating a group, just as update does. The creation form exposes aliasLevelOptions and group.asJSON sends the selected alias_level, but create saves only name and visible. A newly created group therefore retains the default alias level instead of the administrator's selection.

issues.descricao: Removing a member deletes the membership row directly and skips clearing the user's primary_group_id, so a removed user can keep this group as their primary group.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: remove_member uses group.users.delete(user_id) instead of the Group#remove destroy path. WHY: bypasses GroupUser destroy callbacks and primary_group_id cleanup done in destroy_deletions, leaving stale membership side-effects (e.g. dangling primary_group_id). HOW: load the User and call group.remove(user).

Removing a member with group.users.delete bypasses the primary_group_id cleanup previously performed by Group#destroy_deletions during usernames updates. A user whose primary group is this group remains associated with it as their primary group after membership removal, leaving stale primary-group state used by user administration and post serialization. Clear primary_group_id for the removed user when it equals this group's id as part of the removal operation.

issues.descricao: The remove_member spec issues a PUT request although the route only maps DELETE to remove_member, so the test uses a verb never routed in production.
issues.textoGolden: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

comentarios.texto: This example sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the PR maps `remove_member` only to DELETE (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`); PUT on that path routes to `groups#add_members`. Controller specs bypass the router, so the example still lands on `remove_member` and passes regardless — it would still pass if the DELETE route were missing or wired to the wrong action, leaving the newly introduced verb/action pairing untested. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member`, as the sibling example at line 125 already does.

The test 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the route is `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`. It exercises the action with a verb that is never routed in production. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` so the test matches the real request.

issues.descricao: Admin add_members pushes every username into group.users without skipping existing members, so adding someone already in the group hits the unique group_users index, returns a 500 and leaves earlier users partially added.
The public group members endpoint takes `limit` from params with no upper bound or positivity check, letting a visitor request huge pages or trigger a 500 with a negative limit.
Admin remove_member calls group.users.delete with a raw integer id, which raises RecordNotFound (404/500) when the user is not or no longer a member, e.g. on concurrent removal.
Admin remove_member deletes memberships with group.users.delete, which skips GroupUser callbacks, so the cached groups.user_count is never decremented and stays inflated.
Group member pagination is off by one when user_count is a multiple of limit: Next moves to offset == user_count and shows an empty page.
`add_members` runs one User query per username; load all users with a single `User.where(username: ...)` query.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Global group management is authorized with only the VIEW scope. WHY: GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls requireManage(), so an admin granted only all-groups VIEW can create top-level groups, escalating view permission into manage permission. HOW: Change the fallback in canManage() to require only AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, matching ClientPermissionsV2.canManage() and UserPermissionsV2 global canManage().

WHAT: Group listing re-evaluates the global all-groups permission for every group. WHY: Replacing the canViewGlobal short-circuit with groupsEvaluator::canView means V2 calls canView() global (which evaluates the all-groups policy) inside canView(GroupModel) once per group, causing O(N) redundant policy evaluations. HOW: Reintroduce a one-time global canView check before filtering, or cache the global result inside the stream pipeline.

WHAT: Subgroup listing re-evaluates the global all-groups permission for every subgroup. WHY: The filter changed from canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g) to auth.groups()::canView, so V2 re-runs the all-groups policy evaluation for each subgroup instead of short-circuiting once. HOW: Restore the one-time global canView check before the per-group filter.

WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of the actual group IDs. WHY: UserModel.GROUPS is used by JpaUserProvider to filter users by group membership, so resource IDs cause the pre-filter to match nothing and UsersResource.getUsersCount to return the full realm user count for a restricted admin. HOW: Use the resource name (which equals the group id) for both the permission check and the returned set.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, so an admin with only view permission on all groups passes manage checks such as group creation.
issues.textoGolden: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

comentarios.texto: The no-arg canManage() returns true when the caller holds only an all-groups VIEW permission (`hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`), whereas the per-group canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) requires MANAGE. WHAT: a caller with only the view scope on all groups is treated as having manage rights. WHY: canManage()/requireManage() gate group creation and other manage operations (e.g. GroupsResource.addGroup -> auth.groups().requireManage()), so a read-only viewer of all groups can create/manage groups — privilege escalation. HOW: drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() only returns true for MANAGE, aligning it with canManage(GroupModel): `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70) evaluates hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), identical to canView() at line 52, so a caller granted only the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is treated as a group manager. The per-group overload canManage(GroupModel) (line 79) correctly requires only MANAGE, and AdminPermissionsSchema defines MANAGE as the manage scope for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so the two checks disagree. requireManage() therefore succeeds for read-only administrators, letting them create/update/delete groups, add subgroups and map group roles. Drop VIEW from the scope list so canManage() checks MANAGE only.

WHAT: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() grants global manage on VIEW scope (hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)). WHY: A caller with only view-all-groups permission passes the manage check, allowing group creation/management reserved for manage. HOW: Check only MANAGE, e.g. hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

issues.descricao: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses the authorization resource id instead of the resource name (the group id) for both the permission check and the returned set, so per-group view-members grants are not resolved and user filtering gets wrong ids.
issues.textoGolden: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses authz resource IDs (groupResource.getId()) as group IDs and looks them up via findByName. WHY: Resource names equal group IDs (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId()), so findByName(resourceId) misses and the returned set contains unusable IDs, breaking user search/count filtering by group. HOW: Use groupResource.getName() like V1 does (resource.getName().substring prefix / name) for both the hasPermission lookup and the granted set.

findByType callback passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and granted set, but AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup defines resource name (not UUID) as groupId and hasPermission looks up via findByName(server, groupId). Use groupResource.getName() for both check and granted set, otherwise lookups miss to all-groups fallback and callers receive authz UUIDs instead of group IDs.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses groupResource.getId() for lookup and result collection, but V2 group resources are named with the group ID (resolveGroup returns group.getId()) and hasPermission does findByName. Use groupResource.getName() in both places to evaluate the correct per-group resource and to return actual group IDs.

issues.descricao: Per-group resources are created without the Groups type, so getGroupIdsWithViewPermission's findByType never sees specific group grants.

comentarios.texto: findByType(GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) does not enumerate the specific group resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource, because that method creates them without setting their type. Consequently, specific VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are omitted from the group IDs used for user counts and database filtering. Assign the Groups type to specific group resources and ensure the all-Groups resource is not treated as a model group.

issues.descricao: The user search filter still requires legacy 'group.resource.<id>' resources, so with V2 group permissions the members of authorized groups are excluded from user searches.

comentarios.texto: The new V2 group permission IDs are passed into a JPA filter that still requires a legacy group.resource.<groupId> authorization resource. JpaUserProvider.groupsWithPermissionsSubquery checks for that prefixed name, whereas AdminPermissionsSchema creates V2 group resources named only with the group ID, so authorized group members are excluded from user searches even with valid group IDs. Update the database filtering path to support V2 resource naming rather than requiring a legacy V1 resource.

issues.descricao: The new Javadoc for requireManageMembers points to canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers.

comentarios.texto: The javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws ForbiddenException if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false, but this method is the require-variant of canManageMembers, not canManageMembership. The text was copied from requireManageMembership above it. It should reference canManageMembers so the documented contract matches the method name and behavior.

The Javadoc for requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false. It should refer to canManageMembers(GroupModel), which is a different check, so the doc misdescribes the method.

Javadoc for requireManageMembers references canManageMembership instead of canManageMembers (copy-paste). Fix link to {@link #canManageMembers(GroupModel)} so the contract describes the method it guards.

issues.descricao: The Javadoc of getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a Stream though the method returns a Set.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc for getGroupIdsWithViewPermission says it returns a 'Stream of IDs', but the method returns Set<String>. Change the @return text to describe a Set of group IDs.
@return says 'Stream of IDs' but method returns Set<String> getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. Fix doc to 'Set of IDs' to match the signature.

The new @return documentation promises a Stream of IDs, but the method declares Set<String> and both implementations return sets. Describe a set of IDs instead, so the documented return contract matches what callers actually receive.

issues.descricao: GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission runs a full permission evaluation for every group resource on each user search and count, costing O(groups) policy evaluations per request.

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission passes getResourceTypeResource's result to policyStore.findByResource without a null check, causing an NPE and 500 on group listing and user search when the Groups type resource is missing.

Removing the canViewGlobal short-circuit from the subgroup and group listings makes an admin with an all-groups V2 grant run one full authorization evaluation per group in the listing instead of a single check.
GroupPermissionEvaluator.canView() Javadoc promises VIEW/MANAGE permission grants access, but the V1 GroupPermissions implementation only checks admin roles.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads the active device count, compares it to the limit, and then decides whether to insert or update, creating a time-of-check/time-of-use window. WHY: Two concurrent anonymous authentication requests with different device IDs can both see count < limit and both insert rows, so the configured anonymousDeviceLimit can be exceeded. HOW: Wrap the count check and the insert/update in a transaction and serialize concurrent limit checks with SELECT FOR UPDATE on a sentinel row or an advisory lock, so only one request can pass the threshold at a time.

WHAT: When anonymousDeviceLimit is enabled, every anonymous authentication performs a synchronous SELECT COUNT(*) before the upsert. WHY: Previously tagging ran asynchronously in a goroutine with a detached timeout; the new path blocks the auth request on an extra DB round-trip plus the write, increasing latency and load on the anon_device table for every anonymous request. HOW: Cache the active device count with a short TTL and only run the expensive count/conditional update when the cache indicates the limit may be near, or keep the existing async tagging path and only enforce the limit synchronously while logging other tagging failures.

WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads the active device count and then decides whether to insert, with no serialization between the count and the write. WHY: Two concurrent anonymous requests can both observe count < limit and both insert new devices, so the stored device count can exceed anonymousDeviceLimit. HOW: Wrap the count and the conditional insert/update in a single database session with a locking read such as SELECT COUNT(*) ... FOR UPDATE, or use an advisory lock, so the count cannot change between the check and the write.

WHAT: tagDeviceUI writes the local cache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs, and TagDevice now returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. WHY: A device rejected because the limit is reached still has its key cached for 29 minutes, so the next request from the same device hits the cache, skips the database check, and is authenticated. HOW: Move a.localCache.SetDefault to after CreateOrUpdateDevice returns nil so only successfully tagged devices are cached.

WHAT: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever RowsAffected() == 0, but on SQLite a matching UPDATE that sets identical values reports zero rows changed. WHY: When the device limit is reached, a legitimate existing device can be rejected if its client_ip, user_agent and updated_at are unchanged, because the code cannot distinguish 'row not found' from 'row matched but not modified'. HOW: When RowsAffected is 0, run a SELECT for device_id in the active window and only return ErrDeviceLimitReached if the device is absent.

issues.descricao: The device limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate non-atomic steps, so concurrent requests from new devices can all pass the check and exceed the configured limit.
issues.textoGolden: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

comentarios.texto: The limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate steps with no lock or transaction. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit is exceeded. Make the count-and-insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit.

The device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by an insert. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the number of devices exceeds deviceLimit. Make the check and insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit, or serialize the check and insert under a lock.

WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice does check-then-act (CountDevices then INSERT/UPSERT) with no lock, transaction, or unique-guard when deviceLimit>0. WHY: Two concurrent new-device requests can both observe count < limit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit and breaking the enforcement contract. HOW: Enforce atomically (e.g., conditional insert guarded by count in one statement/transaction with serializable lock, or re-check count on conflict).

issues.descricao: Device slots are keyed by the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header with no validation or rate limiting, so an anonymous caller can fill the limit with fake IDs and deny anonymous access to every new legitimate device.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Device slots counted toward deviceLimit are keyed by the unauthenticated X-Grafana-Device-Id header (read in impl.go TagDevice) with no validation or rate-limit. WHY: Any anonymous caller can mint arbitrary device IDs to fill the table up to the limit, after which all legitimate new anonymous devices get ErrDeviceLimitReached and authentication is denied — a trivial anonymous-access DoS introduced by the limit. HOW: Do not let a single client consume many slots (e.g., bind slot consumption to IP/fingerprint, rate-limit new-device creation, or require proof of distinct device).

issues.descricao: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit and never verifies that an existing device can still be updated at the limit.

comentarios.texto: The at-limit call reuses a brand-new device ID ("keep") that was never inserted, so it only reaches updateDevice's `rowsAffected == 0` -> ErrDeviceLimitReached branch. The success branch of the newly added updateDevice (an existing device still being updated while the store is at the limit) is never exercised by any test — every other call uses deviceLimit 0, so updateDevice is never invoked. A regression that made updateDevice always affect 0 rows, use a wrong WHERE/SET, or unconditionally return ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever limit>0 would leave this and all other tests green. Add a case that, after the store is at the limit, calls CreateOrUpdateDevice again with the SAME DeviceID and asserts require.NoError (and ideally that client_ip/user_agent/updated_at were changed), so the update path is actually verified.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit. It would still pass if updateDevice always returned ErrDeviceLimitReached, because it never re-submits the existing device (DeviceID "32mdo31deeqwes") at the limit. Add a call that updates the existing device with a new UserAgent or UpdatedAt, require NoError, and check the stored row changed.

issues.descricao: tagDeviceUI caches the device key before CreateOrUpdateDevice; when the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached the entry stays, so the next request from the same device skips the limit check and authenticates for up to 29 minutes.
issues.textoGolden: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: TagDevice failures that triggered the new ErrDeviceLimitReached early-return are not permanent, because tagDeviceUI (impl.go:87) writes the device key into localCache BEFORE CreateOrUpdateDevice (impl.go:93) and never evicts it on error; tagDeviceUI returns early on any cache hit (impl.go:83-84). WHY: the first request from a new over-limit device is denied, but the poisoned cache makes every subsequent request from that same device skip the limit check entirely and authenticate successfully, so the configurable device limit is bypassed by simply retrying. HOW: only set the cache key after CreateOrUpdateDevice returns nil (e.g. move a.localCache.SetDefault after the successful DB write, or delete the key when it returns ErrDeviceLimitReached).

TagDevice now propagates ErrDeviceLimitReached to deny an over-limit anonymous device, but tagDeviceUI (impl.go:83-95) records the device in localCache at line 87 *before* calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store rejects the device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key is already cached, so the next request for that same device returns early at line 83 with a nil error and the device is admitted. The limit therefore only blocks the first request and is silently bypassed on retry. Fix by only setting the cache entry after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (move SetDefault after the store call), or by removing/not caching the key on failure.

The new authentication gate accepts retries from devices that were rejected by the limit because tagDeviceUI inserts the cache entry before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds. At capacity, the first request with a new X-Grafana-Device-Id fails, but subsequent requests with that same ID hit the 29-minute cache and receive an anonymous identity without admission to the device store. Cache only successful admissions, and ensure concurrent requests cannot treat an in-progress admission as successful.

issues.descricao: Device tagging now runs synchronously in Authenticate, adding DB round-trips on cache-miss anonymous requests where it used to be fire-and-forget.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Anonymous.Authenticate changed from fire-and-forget goroutine TagDevice to synchronous TagDevice(ctx) that runs CountDevices + INSERT/UPDATE inline. WHY: Every cache-miss anonymous authentication now blocks on two DB round-trips in the login hot path, adding latency and DB load per request where previously auth returned immediately. HOW: Restore async tagging for the non-limit path or at least decouple denial from the hot path (e.g., async count with cached count, or only synchronously enforce when near limit).

issues.descricao: The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting has no entry in conf/defaults.ini, so the GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT environment override is ignored and the limit stays 0.
